metadata.title: Week 7 Technical Learnings — Frontend Architecture & Delivery Concepts
metadata.source: Fellow-supplied 7-slide narration script (frontend build-time config, SPA routing fallback, static serving, Vitest/RTL testing strategy, app versioning), provided 2026-10-22. No garbled fragments this time -- narration is verbatim throughout. A STEM/learning-only week: no separate project-update video was supplied alongside this one.
metadata.description: Five frontend-specific delivery concepts: Vite's build-time (not runtime) environment-variable resolution and why each environment needs its own build, the SPA routing fallback that lets a client-side router take over from the web server, serving compiled static assets through a lightweight server like Nginx instead of Node/a dev server, the Vitest + React Testing Library testing strategy that checks behavior rather than implementation details, and baking a version identifier into the build so a running app can report exactly what's live.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- Claude cream skin, slide 1 title card
beats.narration_text: This week's learning focus turned to the frontend side specifically — how a modern React and Vite application is actually configured, built, served, and tested once it leaves your local machine.

beats.role_note: slide 2 -- Vite resolves env vars at build time, not runtime
beats.narration_text: A key concept here is that Vite resolves environment variables at build time, not at runtime. That means values like the backend API URL get compiled directly into the static JavaScript bundle during the build step — there's no server-side process reading environment variables when the app is running. This is different from a typical backend service, and it's why each environment needs its own build rather than one build that reconfigures itself later.

nodes.d: e.g. VITE_API_URL, present only at build time
resolves and compiles values directly into the bundle
config baked in — nothing reads env vars at runtime

props.caption: Each environment needs its own build — there's no reconfiguring a running bundle later.

beats.narration_text: Because this is a single-page application, all the routing logic lives in the browser, not on the server. That means the web server needs to be configured to serve index.html for any path it doesn't recognize as a static file, letting the client-side application take over from there. Without that fallback rule, refreshing the page on any route other than the home page would simply break.

nodes.d: a client-side route, not a real file
doesn't recognize the path as a static file
routing logic lives in the browser

props.caption: Without the fallback rule, refreshing any non-home route would simply break.

beats.role_note: slide 4 -- Nginx, not Node/a dev server, at runtime
beats.narration_text: Once built, a frontend application is just static files — HTML, JavaScript, and CSS. Serving those through a lightweight web server like Nginx, rather than through Node.js or a dev server, is both faster and more secure, since none of the build tooling or source code needs to exist in the running container at all.

nodes.d: HTML, JavaScript, CSS — nothing else needed
lightweight, faster and more secure than Node/a dev server
receives the same static files every time

props.caption: No build tooling or source code needs to exist in the running container at all.

beats.narration_text: On the testing side, the frontend uses Vitest alongside React Testing Library — Vitest as the fast test runner, and React Testing Library for rendering components and verifying behavior the way a real user would interact with them, rather than testing internal implementation details. This is what allows the CI pipeline to catch broken logic or broken UI behavior automatically, before it ever reaches staging.

nodes.d: catches broken logic/UI before it reaches staging

props.caption: Tests the way a real user interacts with the app — not internal implementation details.

beats.narration_text: The build process also bakes in a version identifier at build time, so the running application can report exactly which version is live. This small detail matters a lot operationally — it's what makes it possible to confidently confirm which release is actually running in any given environment, especially after a rollback.

nodes.d: resolved and baked in at build time
the version identifier is part of the bundle
especially valuable right after a rollback

props.caption: A small detail that matters a lot operationally -- confirm, don't assume, what's running.

beats.role_note: slide 7 -- the closing line, Claude cream skin
beats.narration_text: The throughline this week was recognizing that a frontend application has its own distinct deployment considerations — build-time configuration, routing fallback, and lightweight static serving — that are just as deliberate and important as anything on the backend.

props.artifactHeading: A frontend isn't just UI — it's a build artifact with its own deployment rules.
artifactLines: Build-time config: Vite bakes env vars into the bundle — each environment needs its own build.
SPA routing: the server falls back to index.html; the browser's router takes it from there.
Static serving: a lightweight server like Nginx, no build tooling in the running container.
Testing: Vitest + React Testing Library check real user behavior, not implementation details.
Versioning: a build-time identifier lets a running app report exactly what's live.
